newsitem.title: USA: Valujet to buy AirWays, will drop name.
newsitem.headline: Valujet to buy AirWays, will drop name.

text.p: The ValuJet Airlines name, indelibly linked to an airplane's deadly plunge into the swamps of the Florida Everglades, is to disappear when the low-cost airline buys AirWays Corp. in a deal announced Thursday.
The two airlines said they will form a new holding company that will be called AirTran Holdings Inc.
ValuJet has struggled to regain passengers and profitability since its Atlanta-bound Flight 592 crashed shortly after takeoff from Miami on May 11, 1996, killing all 110 passengers and crew on board.
ValuJet President Joseph Corr and AirWays Chairman Robert Swenson told a news conference in Orlando, Fla., that the merger was put together because it made good economic sense.
However, Corr acknowledged the likely merits of dropping the ValuJet name.
"The merger is driven by the economic side. Make no mistake about that," Corr said. "By putting the two companies together it is much more viable economically."

He added, though: "The AirTran name offers us a much better opportunity of going forward. It basically came down to one name or another. We felt AirTran better represented the newness of the company."
The deal calls for ValuJet, based in Atlanta, to acquire Orlando-based AirWays in a one-for-one stock swap.
ValuJet will also issue about 9.07 million shares of stock valued at about $61.8 million, based on ValuJet's closing stock price of $6.81 on Wednesday.
The combination has been structured as a tax-free merger, the companies said.
The Everglades disaster raised numerous questions about ValuJet's safety procedures.

Preliminary reports indicated the crash was caused by a fire in the cargo hold ignited by oxygen generating canisters that had been mislabeled and improperly secured. The National Transportation Safety Board's final report is expected later this month.

The final merger and closing date are expected to occur within three to four months. The company will initially be based in Orlando, where AirWays has maintenance facilities, and the Florida city is a leading candidate to be chosen as the permanent base.
The combined company will have 2,742 employees and serve 46 cities with 238 peak daily departures and a fleet of 40 aircraft.
"We both emphasise affordable fares. We will continue to bring affordable fares to the people of this nation," Swenson said.
AirWays' AirTran Airways currently provides service between Orlando and 23 cities with a fleet of Boeing 737 aircraft. It expects delivery of its 11th Boeing 737 aircraft by the end of July.
ValuJet Airlines currently operates 200 systemwide peak daily departures to 24 cities with a fleet of 30 aircraft.
Corr, who joined ValuJet last November, will serve as president and chief executive officer. Swenson, now CEO as well as chairman at Airways, will become non-executive chairman.

Other executives will be chosen from the "most dedicated and most talented" of the two companies' present employees, Corr said, adding he did not expect many job losses because neither company is overstaffed.
Both carriers, AirTran Airways and ValuJet Airlines, will continue to function under their respective operating certificates, the companies said.
AirWays' stock gained $1.375 to $6.75, while ValueJet was up 81.25 cents at $7.625, both in afternoon trading on Nasdaq.
